events.text: Before choosing a research direction, I need the lab's rules for running experiments and publishing contributions. I'll start with the guide.
The guide is clear. Next I'll look at the data layout, the README files, and the baselines so I can choose a direction the evaluator can test on held-out data.

I'll read the baseline code and the DOMAIN file before picking a direction, since the evaluator's comparator is what a `prediction` claim has to beat.

```bash
cat /lab/data/baselines/compbio_baseline.py; echo ---; cat /lab/data/baselines/README.md; echo ---; ls -la /lab/data/DOMAIN; head -c 1500 /lab/data/DOMAIN/* 2>/dev/null | head -80; echo ---; cat /lab/data/GUIDE.md | head -60; echo ---; head -5 /lab/data/BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014/train.csv; cat /lab/data/BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014/meta.json | head -40
```

I'll check the installed Python packages, core count, the time budget, and whether `lab datasets` shows the evaluator's held-out input format before writing any model code.


```bash
python -c "import sklearn, numpy, pandas; print(sklearn.__version__, numpy.__version__, pandas.__version__)"; python -c "import lightgbm; print('lgbm', lightgbm.__version__)" 2>&1 | tail -1; python -c "import xgboost; print('xgb', xgboost.__version__)" 2>&1 | tail -1; nproc; lab datasets; lab budget; wc -l /lab/data/*/train.csv
```

I'll build a position-aware model. The baseline is one-hot ridge, which can't share information across variants at the same position. My features are leave-one-out position means, neighbour-window means, similarity-weighted means over other substitutions at the same site, and physicochemical properties, fed to LightGBM. I'll compare against the ridge baseline with 5-fold CV on the public training data.

```bash
mkdir -p /work/exp1 && cat > /work/exp1/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, sys, json, glob
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection im

The first run shows LightGBM with L1 loss beating the ridge baseline on all seven assays in 5-fold CV. Before I build on it, I'm fixing one problem I spotted in my own features. `pos_min` and `pos_max` include the row's own target during training, so the model sees a leaked value that won't exist at test time. I'll make them leave-one-out, rerun the CV, and check the prediction-mode code path on a local split.

```bash
cd /work/exp1 && python - <<'EOF'
s = open("run.py").read()
old = """            kmin[i] = yj.min(); kmax[i] = yj.max()"""
new = """            kmin[i] = yj.min(); kmax[i] = yj.

The leakage fix I just made was a no-op. The replacement string was identical to the original, so the file is unchanged. The concern itself was also wrong: `loo=True` is only used when `q` is the training table, and the loop drops the row's own index before computing `pos_min`/`pos_max`. The CV numbers stand. I'll check the recorded runs and look at the new prediction output.

```bash
lab runs; echo ---; cd /work/exp1 && sed -n 60,90p run.py | head -40; echo ---; python -c "
import pandas as pd
p=pd.read_csv('/tmp/fe/out/predictions.csv'); print(p.describe())
t=pd.read_csv('/lab/data/BLAT_ECOL

The prediction path has a gap: `run.py` only predicts when given positional args, so a plain `python run.py` in the evaluator would fail. I'll rewrite it so that prediction mode discovers datasets from `EVAL_DIR`, and so the default run reports a true 80/20 holdout alongside the CV. The earlier "leakage fix" changed nothing, so I'm not counting it.

```bash
mkdir -p /work/exp2 && cat > /work/exp2/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, json, glob
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
import lightgbm as lgb

DATA = os.environ["DATA_D

The holdout result holds up. LightGBM with L1 loss beats the ridge comparator on all seven assays on a 20% split of the public training data, and the 5-fold CV agrees. I'll pre-register `lgb_l1` as the single method because CV chose it before the holdout was run. Before publishing prediction-test findings, I'll check that the prediction path works end to end on a mock held-out folder built from a split the model never trains on.

```bash
cd /work/exp2 && rm -rf /tmp/fe2 && mkdir -p /tmp/fe2/BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014 /tmp/fe2/out && python -c "
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
d=pd.read_csv('/la

The holdout result is the only evidence I'll claim from so far. The mock-holdout MAE of 0.103 I just printed is not valid: those 300 rows were in the training set, so it's in-sample and I won't cite it. I'll publish one finding per assay, each citing the holdout exec `exec-a98676e3` and the code blob it ran with.

```bash
cd /work/exp2 && python - <<'EOF'
import json, subprocess
EXEC = "exec-a98676e3"
CODE = "c45c621051fc7a53132726dfaddb13a12ecc2f321210075bc8a74ca258c4833a"
# holdout MAEs copied from exec-a98676e3 metrics.json

The seven findings were recorded, and each passed its live checks. The trailing error came from a stray tag in my command, not from the contributions. I'll confirm the artifact list and inspect one artifact's test spec before deciding what to run next.

```bash
lab artifacts | head -40; echo ---; lab show findin-867ff738 | head -60
```

The seven findings are recorded and live. Before adding more claims, I want to check whether the holdout is truly independent. Exp1's 5-fold CV chose `lgb_l1` using all public rows, including the 20% I used as holdout, so the holdout is not fully clean for model selection. I'll check the message board and budget, then run a nested check that selects the method using only the 80% training portion.

```bash

import os, json, importlib.util, numpy as np, pandas as pd
# reuse exp2

The last command failed to parse because of a stray closing tag, so the nested-selection run never started. I'll rerun it cleanly. The script also read `/work/exp2/run.py` by absolute path, which the evaluator's copy of the directory won't have, so I'll copy the base code into `exp3` and load it relatively.

```bash

from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
src = open("base.py").read().split("if EVAL:")[0]

The nested check confirms the choice. Inside the 80% portion, 5-fold CV selects `lgb_l1` on all seven assays, and the holdout MAEs match exp2 exactly. So the seven findings don't depend on a leaky selection step.

Next I'll test whether a seed-bagged version of the same model, and a shallower and a deeper tree variant, improve on the holdout. I'll choose the variant inside the 80% portion by inner CV and report only the holdout score of the chosen one.


```bash
mkdir -p /work/exp4 && cp /work/exp2/run.py /work/exp4/base.py && cat > /work/exp4/run.py <<'EOF'
import os, json, numpy as np, panda

The variant search gives gains of only 0.001 to 0.002 MAE over the base model, which is inside the noise, so I won't publish it. A larger opportunity is that the two BLAT assays and the two RASK assays measure the same protein. I'll test whether pooling a partner dataset's training variants (rescaled to the target's mean and SD) improves holdout MAE, choosing between own-only and pooled by inner CV on the 80% portion.

```bash
mkdir -p /work/exp5 && cp /work/exp2/run.py /work/exp5/base.py && cat > /work/exp5/run.py <<'EOF'

The run failed on a duplicate `random_state` keyword, because `LGB_PARAMS` already sets it. I'll drop the explicit argument and rerun.

Pooling helps the BLAT pair in both directions (0.1646 to 0.1411 and 0.3764 to 0.3435), and the inner CV picked it for both. It hurts the RASK and KCNE1 pairs, so I'll apply pooling only to the BLAT pair. The partner-pooling method also needs a prediction-mode path before I can claim it as a `prediction` test, so I'll write that now, with a holdout metric mode that reproduces the numbers from the same code.

```bash
